candidates.name: Nieca Goldberg
candidates.narrative: Nieca Goldberg’s interest in cardiology began when her father developed heart disease at a young age. Her NYU biography describes summer work with a cardiologist and a later decision to focus on women after encountering dismissive assumptions about their heart health during residency. Questions from patients also shaped her interest in making space for dialogue: she describes beginning visits by asking what patients want to discuss.
candidates.humanityBasis: Family experience, a documented choice of specialty, and patient-question-centered practice.

candidates.name: Holly S. Andersen
candidates.narrative: Holly Andersen’s public education work reaches beyond the cardiology office. NewYork-Presbyterian’s 2017 announcement identifies her as the leader of its hands-only CPR awareness campaign, built around helping ordinary bystanders feel able to respond to cardiac arrest. The campaign gives her profile a concrete community connection: translating cardiovascular knowledge into something people outside medicine can learn and share.
candidates.humanityBasis: A specific community education project, rather than a generic service description.

candidates.name: Tara Narula
candidates.identityNote: Northwell lists Tara Narula Cangello. Reconcile the institutional and media names before assigning any new ID or route.
candidates.narrative: Tara Narula took an unusual route into medicine. An American Heart Association profile describes how she first started a smoothie business in Miami before returning to medical training. Her later work combines cardiology with medical journalism and public education. In the same interview, she explains a desire to reach people beyond her office and describes discussing everyday stress alongside cardiovascular care.
candidates.humanityBasis: Entrepreneurship-to-medicine journey and an attributed public education motivation.

candidates.name: Anuradha (Anu) Lala-Trindade
candidates.narrative: Anu Lala-Trindade traces her wish to become a cardiologist to a childhood encounter with her grandmother’s illness. In Mount Sinai’s Heart to Heart interview, she recalls feeling her grandmother’s pulse and becoming fascinated by the connection between the heartbeat and a person’s life. She also describes the importance of human connection in caring for patients and supporting families through uncertainty.
candidates.humanityBasis: First-person childhood motivation and a specific account of relationships in care.

candidates.name: Stacy Notaras Murphy
candidates.narrative: Before becoming a counselor, Stacy Notaras Murphy worked as a business writer and editor. Her biography describes bringing those reporting skills into psychology writing for Counseling Today in 2005. An interest in relationships led her toward additional couples work, followed by further study of trauma and its effects on relationships. She also describes meeting with other therapists for continuing consultation and support.
candidates.humanityBasis: Writing-to-counseling journey and a documented continuing-learning motivation.

candidates.name: Kathleen Smith
candidates.narrative: Kathleen Smith carries her interest in relationship patterns into both therapy and writing. Her official biography describes a therapy newsletter as a favorite part of her work and says she enjoys talking with friends about relationships in television shows. Her teaching also brings family-systems ideas to clinicians and other professional groups, giving her public writing and clinical work a shared focus on how people relate to one another.
candidates.humanityBasis: Specific writing interest, television discussion hobby and documented teaching connection.
